All functions in R have at least 3 things: - A *name* (we pick that and use it to call the function) - input *arguments* (one or more comma separated)

creatye a function to `add()` numbers together **Q1a** Your first version of the function should add two input numbers together. For example, add(4, 7) should return 11.

```{r}
add <- function(x,y) {
  x+y
}
```

test our new function

```{r}
add(1,100)
```

```{r}
add(10,1)
```

setting a defualt value for x or y will allow it to process the add function with only one value. input arguments can have defaults

**Q1b** For you second version, adapt your first function so it can take a single input vector or two inputs as before. For example, add(4, 7) and add( c(4,7,10) ). \[1 pt\]

```{r}
add <- function(x, y=0) {
  sum(x, y)
}
```

```{r}
add(c(4,7,10))
```

**Q1c** Finally, on your own (outside of class) create a third version of your function that can add any number of inputs that the user provides. For example, add(1, 2, 3, -4) should return. Hint: explore the... (dots) argument or the base R function sum(). \[2 pts\]

```{r}
add <- function(x, y,z) {
  sum(x,y,z)
}
add(5, 10, 15)
```

## Generate a DNA function

Write a function generate_dna() that returns a random DNA sequence of a length specified by the user.

**Q2a**a. Your first version should return a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides. For example generate_dna(6) might return "A", "T", "T", "G", "A", "C". \[1 pt\]

```{r}
sample(x=1:10, size =1)
```

We can use this woth "A" "C" "G" "T" as input x to make random nucleotide sequences

```{r}
sample(x = c("A","C","T","G"), size = 4, replace = TRUE)
```

this snippet of code can work for the "body" of our first `generate_dna()` function

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len) {sample(x = c("A","C","T","G"), size = len, replace = TRUE)
}
```

```{r}
generate_dna(100)
          
```

**Q2b** b. Your second version should optionally be able to return either a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides (as before) or a single character string (not a vector of single letters but a singe vector of multiple letters). For example "AAGGCTG". \[1 pt\]

```{r}
paste( c("A", "C", "A"), collapse = "")
```

```{r}
flag <- FALSE
if(flag) {
  cat ("look at me! we are in here")
} else {
  cat("Nooo")
}
```

changing the true or flase changes what gets printed out

combine these two things to improve the function

```{r}
generate_dna <-function(len, fasta=TRUE) {#collapse changed to fasta 
  s <- sample(x=c("A","C","T","G"),size=len,replace=TRUE) 
  if(fasta) {
  s <- paste(s, collapse="")
    #cat("You picked True!!")
  return(s)}
}
```

```{r}
generate_dna(6, fasta = T)
```

**Q2c** Finally, create a final version of your function that prints out a FASTA format sequence with an id line indicating the sequence length. For example:

```{r}
len <- 90
paste (">length",len,sep="")
```

```{r}
generate_dna <-function(len, fasta=FALSE) {
  #multi element nucleotide vector
  s <- sample(x=c("A","C","T","G"),size=len,replace=TRUE) 
  
  if(fasta) {
    #make a single element vector
  s <- paste(s, collapse="")
  
  #add a FASTA >id line
  id <- paste(">length", len, sep ="")
  s <- paste(id,s,sep ="\n")
  cat(s)}
  return(s)
  }
```

```{r}
x <- generate_dna(9, fasta = T)
```

**Q3** Write a function generate_protein() that returns a random peptide/protein sequence of a length specified by the user. For example generate_protein(6) might return "WQRTAG". Your function should: Use the single-letter code for all 20 standard amino acids and no other letters (see earlier list at the beginning of this handout)and include clear comments that explain each step of your function. \[2 pts\]

```{r}
aa <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "E", "Q", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S","T", "W", "Y", "V")
```

```{r}
generate_protein <- function(len, fasta=FALSE) {
  #multi element amino acid vector
  s <- sample(x=aa,size=len,replace=TRUE)
  if(fasta) {
  #add a FASTA >id line
    s <- paste(s, collapse = "")
id <- paste(">length", len, sep ="")
s <- paste(id,s, "\n", sep ="\n")
  cat(s)}
  return(s) }
```

```{r}
x <- generate_protein(6, fasta = T)
```

```{r}
x <- generate_protein(7, fasta =T)
x <- generate_protein(8, fasta =T)
```

**Q4** Adapt and use your generate_protein() function to generate a series of random protein sequences ranging from 6 to 13 amino acids in length (one sequence per length). Take advantage of the base R function for() or sapply() so that you do not have to call generate_protein() eight times by hand. we can do a `for()` loop

```{r}
for(len in 6:13) {
  #cat("length =",len, "\n")
  x <- generate_protein(len, fasta =T)
}
```

```{r}
sapply(3:13, generate_protein, fasta =T)
```

**Q5** BLASTp search against nr — are your peptides “unique in nature”? Take your FASTA-formatted peptides from Q4 and run them as a single BLASTp search against the Non-redundant protein sequences (nr) database at https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/. For this question do not restrict the organism (leave the Organism field blank so that the full nr database is searched).

| Length(aa) | Best Hit % identity | Best Hit % Coverage | Unique? (Y/N) |
|------------|---------------------|---------------------|---------------|
| 6          | 100                 | 100                 | N             |
| 7          | 100                 | 100                 | N             |
| 8          | 100                 | 100                 | N             |
| 9          | 100                 | 89                  | Y             |
| 10         | 90                  | 100                 | Y             |
| 11         | 90.91               | 91                  | Y             |
| 12         | 90                  | 83                  | Y             |
| 13         | 83.3                | 92                  | Y             |

**Q5a**At which sequence length do your randomly generated peptides start to look “unique in nature” (i.e. no 100% coverage + 100% identity hit)? \[1 pt\]

The randomly generated peptides start looking "unique" in nature starting at length = 9. As the petide sequence gets longer there is lesser percent identity matches and query coverage.

**Q5b**b. Speculate why very short random peptides are almost always found in nr, while longer ones typically are not. Your answer should refer both to the size of the sequence space (20𝐿 for a peptide of length 𝐿) and to the size of the known protein universe. \[1 pt\]

Shorter,random peptides are found in nr because the length is very short, therefore the randomness gives more chances of the short length peptide chain being found in more proteins. Longer chains are less reliant on *chance* and more reliable over all. The odds of a 12 amino acids chain being in a specific protein in that specific sequence are very low compared to 3 amino acids in a row.

**Q6** In 3–6 sentences total and using your Q5 data and the reasoning from Q5b, what do you think this minimum length is and why might it be a bad design choice for the immune system to present very short peptides?

According to my data the shortest possible length can be length = 8 peptide. However this cannot be presumed to be the exact length for the MHC class II molecule. In this design assuming length = 8, a T helper cell will detect a foreign body automatically when it detects an 8 length peptide and activate an immune response. This is not a great design for the immune system since short peptide chains may present randomly (more often than intentionally). What I mean is the chances of a short chain protein being presented in the molecule is high and will be difficult to differentiate self and foreign bodies and with the mechanism of T helper-cells analyzing these sequences as foreign may set off an immune response even when NOT necessary. It is more relaible to distinguish "self" vs "non-self" from longer chain proteins as they are more specialized and unique and have alesser chance of being random.
